introduction-the-price-of-performance.core: Resource settings drive both cost and reliability: requests too high waste nodes, too low cause noisy neighbours and evictions; limits too low throttle or kill Pods. The goal is the 'Goldilocks zone', with requests matching real usage, sensible limits and autoscaling to follow demand.

first_principles.problem: A cluster runs at 25% real utilisation yet Pods are throttled and OOM-killed.

analogy.title: Booking restaurant tables
analogy.story: Book for 10 when 4 come and you waste seats; book for 2 when 6 come and people stand.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants can add chairs; nodes can't stretch beyond their capacity.

check.q: What's the cost of setting requests far above real usage?
check.a: Wasted node capacity, since the scheduler reserves resources that aren't used.

requests-vs-limits-the-contract.core: Requests are the guaranteed amount used for scheduling and fair sharing under contention; limits are hard caps enforced by the kernel (cgroups). CPU requests set cpu.weight shares and CPU limits set CFS quota. Memory requests influence eviction ranking and memory limits set memory.max for OOM kills.

first_principles.problem: Engineers assume a Pod can't use more than its request, or that requests cap usage.

analogy.title: A guaranteed salary plus an overtime cap
analogy.story: You always get the base, may earn more when there's work, but never beyond the cap.
analogy.breaks: Salaries don't get killed for exceeding caps; memory over the limit does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See exactly how settings are enforced.

check.q: Can a container use more CPU than its request?
check.a: Yes, it can burst up to its limit (or node capacity if no limit) when CPU is available.

the-consequences-of-hitting-limits.core: Hitting a CPU limit throttles the container: it waits until the next CFS period, adding latency but no crash. Hitting a memory limit triggers an OOM kill (exit code 137, OOMKilled), followed by restarts and possibly CrashLoopBackOff. Node-level memory pressure evicts Pods by QoS and usage over request.

first_principles.problem: A service's p99 latency spikes every few seconds, and nobody connects it to CPU throttling.
derivation: Fix **memory leaks** rather than endlessly raising limits.

analogy.title: A speed governor versus a fuse
analogy.story: The governor slows you down; the fuse cuts the power entirely.
analogy.breaks: Fuses can be reset manually; OOM-killed containers restart automatically, maybe in a loop.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Heap leak fixed; limit set with 25% headroom.

check.q: What exit code indicates a container was OOM-killed?

deep-dive-cfs-quota-and-cpu-throttling.core: CPU limits use CFS bandwidth control: a quota of CPU time per period (default 100 ms). A 0.5-CPU limit allows 50 ms per period across all threads, so a multi-threaded app can burn its quota in 10 ms and then stall for 90 ms, causing latency spikes even when average usage is low. Many teams drop CPU limits for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests.

first_principles.problem: A 4-thread service with a 1-CPU limit shows 30% average CPU but frequent 80 ms stalls.
truths: Quota is shared by all threads.
derivation: **Remove or raise CPU limits** for latency-sensitive apps.
Match **thread pools** to CPU allocation (GOMAXPROCS, JVM settings).
Use **Guaranteed + static CPU manager** for exclusive cores.

analogy.title: A phone plan with minutes per hour
analogy.story: Use them all in the first ten minutes and you can't call for the rest of the hour.
analogy.breaks: Phone plans reset hourly; CFS resets every 100 ms, so stalls are short but frequent.

example.title: Throttle maths
flow: 4 threads busy → quota used in 25 ms

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Remove CPU limit; set GOMAXPROCS from request.

check.q: Why can a container be throttled while its average CPU usage is low?
check.a: Multi-threaded bursts can consume the per-period quota quickly, causing stalls until the next period.

quality-of-service-classes-how-kubernete.core: QoS classes rank Pods for eviction under node pressure. Guaranteed (requests = limits for CPU and memory) are evicted last, Burstable in order of usage above requests, and BestEffort (no settings) first. The kubelet's eviction thresholds (memory.available, nodefs.available) trigger eviction before the kernel OOM killer acts.

first_principles.problem: Critical Pods get evicted first because they have no requests set.

analogy.title: Lifeboat boarding order
analogy.story: Crew essential to the ship stay, passengers with tickets next, stowaways first off.
analogy.breaks: Lifeboats are rare; evictions happen routinely on busy nodes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Nodes evict gracefully before system processes starve.

check.q: Why reserve resources for system and kube daemons on nodes?
check.a: So kubelet, the runtime and OS processes aren't starved by Pods, keeping the node healthy.

autoscaling-wars-vpa-vs-hpa.core: HPA scales the number of replicas based on metrics (CPU or memory utilisation relative to requests, custom or external metrics). VPA recommends or applies per-Pod request changes (vertical sizing), historically by restarting Pods, with in-place resize emerging. Don't let both act on the same CPU/memory metric; common combos are VPA in recommendation mode plus HPA, or HPA on custom metrics plus VPA on resources.

first_principles.problem: HPA and VPA fight: VPA raises requests, lowering utilisation, so HPA scales in, and the loop oscillates.
truths: Horizontal and vertical scaling solve different problems.
derivation: Use **custom metrics** (RPS, queue depth) for HPA.

analogy.title: Hiring more staff versus giving staff bigger desks
analogy.story: More staff handles more customers; bigger desks help each person work better. Doing both by the same measure confuses things.
analogy.breaks: Hiring takes weeks; Pods scale in seconds, so feedback loops can oscillate quickly.

steps.label: Pair
steps.detail: VPA in Off mode gives request recommendations.

check.q: Why shouldn't HPA and VPA both act on CPU utilisation?
check.a: VPA changing requests alters the utilisation HPA uses, causing conflicting, oscillating decisions.

setting-the-right-values-a-practical-fra.core: A practical framework: observe usage over representative periods (including peaks), set CPU requests near P90 usage, memory requests near P99 with limits ~20–30% higher, generally avoid CPU limits for latency-sensitive services (or set them generously), load-test, use VPA recommendations and tools like Goldilocks or Kubecost, enforce defaults with LimitRanges and review regularly.

first_principles.problem: Teams guess resource values once and never revisit them.

analogy.title: Tailoring a suit from measurements, then refitting
analogy.story: Measure properly, allow some room and adjust as you change.
analogy.breaks: People change slowly; workloads change with every release.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Efficient and safe settings backed by data.

check.q: Why set memory limits somewhat above requests?
check.a: To allow occasional spikes without OOM kills while still capping runaway usage.
